- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.7) and forecast is significantly above recent mean, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.3) and forecast is below recent mean, increase forecast by 5–10% to avoid underreaction.  
- If recent price spike is followed by forecast overshoot, apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day for 3–5 days post-spike.  
- If forecast mean reversion is delayed (e.g., 3–5 days after peak), adjust downward by 1–3% per day until convergence with true trend.  
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.7), use 3–5 day moving average of recent 10-day price to anchor forecast.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated overestimation in bullish periods, apply a “sentiment decay” rule: reduce forecast by 2–5% for each consecutive bullish sentiment day.  
- If forecast consistently misses true outcome by +2% or more in early days (1–7), apply “early correction” — reduce forecast by 1–3% per day until convergence.  
- If forecast consistently misses by -2% or more in late days (20–30), apply “late correction” — increase forecast by 1–3% per day to catch up.
